groups.name: Your body
groups.line: Moving it, making it strong, and what it can do in water.

groups.name: The outdoors
groups.line: Fire, weather, wild things, and everything above your head.

groups.name: Your mind
groups.line: Numbers, words, memory, seeing properly, and saying what you mean.

groups.name: Making things
groups.line: With your hands, with a tune, and with a bit of misdirection.

groups.name: Everyday life
groups.line: Feeding people, earning, fixing, caring, and keeping your head.

categories.name: Body and movement
categories.line: Juggling, skipping, upside down, breath, strength, speed.

tracks.name: Juggling
tracks.line: Three balls in the air, eventually.

steps.test: Throw one ball from hand to hand ten times without dropping it.
how: One ball only. A rolled sock works.
Throw it from your right hand to your left, up to about eye height.
Aim for the same arc every time rather than for speed.
Ten throws without dropping it.

steps.test: Juggle two balls in one hand, twenty throws.
steps.note: Both balls in the SAME hand, going round in a circle. It looks wrong until it suddenly does not.

steps.test: Do a three-ball cascade for ten catches.
steps.note: A cascade means they cross over in the middle, not round in a circle. Ten catches, drops allowed before that.

steps.test: Juggle three balls for thirty seconds with no drop.
Juggle three balls for two whole minutes.
Juggle while walking twenty steps, and teach somebody the first throw.

tracks.name: Skipping
tracks.line: Stepping over a rope to running a game of it.

steps.test: Step over a rope lying still on the ground, ten times.
how: Lay the rope flat on the ground in a straight line.
Step over it and back, ten times, getting quicker.
This teaches your feet where the rope is before it starts moving.

steps.test: Skip ten times in a row without stopping.
steps.note: The rope goes right round and under your feet each time. Little jumps, not big ones.

steps.test: Skip fifty times in a row.
Skip one hundred times in a row.
Skip one hundred with the rope crossed over at least once.
Run a skipping game for the whole group.

tracks.name: Upside down
tracks.line: Rolls, cartwheels, handstands.

steps.test: Do a forward roll and come back up on your feet.
how: Do this on grass or something soft.
Tuck your chin to your chest — that is the whole safety of it.
Push with your legs, roll over the back of your shoulders, and stand up.

steps.test: Do a cartwheel and land on your feet.
steps.note: Sideways, hands down one after the other, legs over. On grass first.

steps.test: Hold a handstand against a wall for thirty seconds.
Cartwheel cleanly in both directions.
Hold a free handstand for ten seconds.
steps.note: Free means nothing to lean on and nobody holding you.

steps.test: Walk five steps on your hands.

tracks.name: Breath
tracks.line: Thirty seconds to two minutes, calmly.

steps.test: Hold your breath for thirty seconds, sitting still.
how: Sit down first. Never do this in water.
Breathe out all the way, then take one big slow breath in.
Hold, and stay still — moving uses it up.
Somebody counts to thirty out loud. Let it go whenever you want to.

steps.test: Breathe in for four, hold four, out for four, ten rounds.
steps.note: In for a count of four, hold four, out for four. Ten times round.

steps.test: Hold your breath for one minute.
Slow your own heart down on purpose and notice it happen.
steps.note: Sit still, breathe slowly out for longer than you breathe in, and feel your pulse at your wrist. It slows.

steps.test: Hold your breath for ninety seconds.
Hold for two minutes, and teach somebody the slow breathing.

tracks.name: Strength
tracks.line: One press-up to carrying somebody.

steps.test: Do one press-up properly, all the way down and up.
Do ten press-ups without stopping.
Hang from a bar for sixty seconds.
Do one pull-up from a dead hang.
Do five pull-ups.
Carry somebody your own size fifty metres.

tracks.name: Running
tracks.line: A hundred metres to an hour.

steps.test: Run one hundred metres flat out.
Run for five minutes without stopping.
Run a mile without walking.
steps.note: A mile is about four times round a running track, or fifteen minutes of walking done as running instead.

steps.test: Run for thirty minutes without stopping.
Run five kilometres.
Run ten kilometres, or run beside somebody doing their first mile.

tracks.name: Balance
tracks.line: A log to a slackline.

steps.test: Walk the length of a log or a low wall without falling off.
how: Find a log, a kerb or a low wall.
Look at where you are going, not at your feet. That is the whole trick.
Walk the length of it. Arms out is allowed.

steps.test: Stand on one foot for a minute with your eyes closed.
Walk heel to toe along a straight line for twenty steps, eyes closed.
Stand up on a slackline or a beam and stay there ten seconds.
steps.note: A slackline is a flat webbing strap between two trees. A gymnastics beam or a fallen tree counts.

steps.test: Walk five metres on a slackline.
Turn round on a slackline and come back.

tracks.name: Riding
tracks.line: Balance bike to a long road.

steps.test: Sit on a bike and push yourself along with your feet.
Ride ten metres without stabilisers or feet down.
Start, stop and steer around things safely.
steps.note: Stopping means using the brakes and putting a foot down where you meant to, not falling off.

steps.test: Ride five miles without stopping.
Ride safely on a road, with the signals and the road sense.
steps.note: Road sense means looking behind, signalling with your arm, and knowing where cars cannot see you.

steps.test: Ride twenty miles in a day.

categories.name: Outdoors and wild
categories.line: Fire, finding your way, shelter, weather, tracks, wild food.

tracks.name: Fire
tracks.line: Gathering sticks to teaching somebody else.

steps.test: Gather a bundle of dry sticks that would actually burn.
how: Look for dead sticks off the ground, never green ones off a tree.
Snap one — if it cracks it is dry, if it bends it is no use.
Gather a bundle as thick as your wrist, in three sizes: matchstick, pencil, thumb.

steps.test: Lay a fire properly so it would light.
steps.note: Laid properly means smallest at the bottom, air gaps all through it, and nothing packed tight.

steps.test: Light it with matches and put it out so nobody could tell.
steps.note: Out properly means cold enough to put your hand in the ashes. Water, then stir, then water again.

steps.test: Cook something on a fire you laid and lit.
Light a fire with no matches and no lighter.
Teach two other people to lay and light one safely.

tracks.name: Finding your way
tracks.line: Pointing north to leading a route.

steps.test: Point which way is north, and be right.
how: In the morning the sun is roughly east, in the evening roughly west.
Stand with your right hand pointing at the morning sun — you are now facing north.
Say out loud which way north is, then check with a phone compass.
Being right is the level. Being close is a good start.

steps.test: Name three landmarks you can see and say which way home is.
steps.note: A landmark is anything you would recognise again — a mast, a church, a big tree on its own, a hill with a shape, a bend in the road, the sea. In the countryside it is often the hill line or which way the ground slopes.

steps.test: Follow a marked path on a map for a mile without being told.
steps.note: A marked path is one drawn on the map — a dotted line, a track, a road. Following it means you always know which bit of the line you are standing on.

steps.test: Navigate a mile with a map and a compass.
steps.note: Set the map so north on the map points at north in real life. Everything gets easier after that.

steps.test: Plan a route yourself and lead the group along it.
Lead a route that takes two days.

tracks.name: Shelter
tracks.line: A den to a night out in it.

steps.test: Build a den big enough to sit inside.
Build one that two people fit in.
Build one that keeps you dry through ten minutes of rain.
Build one you would be warm in overnight, and prove it with a thermometer.
steps.note: Warmer inside than outside is the test. A cheap thermometer inside and one outside settles it.

steps.test: Sleep a whole night in a shelter you built.
Build one with a group and get everybody through the night dry.

tracks.name: Weather and tide
tracks.line: Reading the day before it happens.

steps.test: Dress yourself right for the weather that is actually outside.
Read a forecast and say what everybody should bring.
steps.note: Wind and rain matter more than temperature. Say what to bring, not just what the weather is.

steps.test: Read a tide table and say when the beach will be gone.
steps.note: A tide table tells you the times of high and low water. Low water is when the beach is biggest.

steps.test: Plan a beach walk around the tide and get it right.
Change or call off a plan because of the weather, and explain why.
Keep a group safe and cheerful through genuinely bad weather.

tracks.name: Trees and birds
tracks.line: Five leaves to leading a nature walk.

steps.test: Find five different kinds of leaf and lay them out.
how: Walk anywhere with trees or hedges.
Pick five leaves that all look different from each other.
Lay them out in a row and look at what makes each one different.

steps.test: Name five trees from their leaves alone.
steps.note: Ash, oak, beech, sycamore and hawthorn will cover most hedges here. Shape, edge and stalk are the clues.

steps.test: Name five birds on sight, outdoors, not from a book.
steps.note: Robin, blackbird, magpie, wood pigeon and a gull is an easy first five almost anywhere here.

steps.test: Name ten birds from their call with your eyes shut.
Name twenty wild plants and say which are useful.
Lead a walk and name what you pass as you go.

tracks.name: Wild food
tracks.line: One berry to a whole meal.

steps.test: Pick and eat one wild food with somebody who knows it.
steps.note: Blackberries in autumn are the safe start. Never eat anything an adult who genuinely knows has not seen.

steps.test: Identify three safe wild foods without being told.
Pick enough of something to bring home and cook.
Name five things that would poison you, and why.
steps.note: The ones that matter here: hemlock, foxglove, yew berries, lords and ladies, and any mushroom you are unsure of.

steps.test: Make a meal where three ingredients came from the wild.
Take somebody else foraging and keep them safe.

tracks.name: Tracking
tracks.line: A footprint to following an animal.

steps.test: Find an animal footprint and say what made it.
steps.note: Mud at the edge of a puddle, wet sand, or snow. Look for the shape and count the toes.

steps.test: Follow your own tracks backwards for fifty metres.
Name five animals from their prints or droppings.
Follow an animal trail for two hundred metres.
Read a trail and say what the animal was doing and when.
Sit still long enough that a wild animal comes close on its own.

tracks.name: Camping
tracks.line: The garden to a wild night.

steps.test: Sleep a whole night in a tent in the garden.
Put a tent up on your own.
Pack for a night away from a list and forget nothing.
steps.note: A list means written down before you start, not remembered. Sleeping, warm, dry, food, torch, toothbrush.

steps.test: Camp a night away from the house and cook your own tea.
Camp two nights carrying everything you need.
Take a younger child on their first night out and get them home happy.

categories.name: Water and boats
categories.line: Swimming, cold water, rowing, sailing, fishing, rock pools.

tracks.name: Swimming
tracks.line: Face in the water to open water.

steps.test: Put your face in the water and blow bubbles.
how: Somewhere shallow, with somebody with you.
Big breath, face in, and blow out slowly through your nose.
Bubbles you can see. Come up whenever you like.

steps.test: Float on your back for ten seconds.
steps.note: On your back, ears in the water, chin up, breathing normally. Somebody stands beside you.

steps.test: Swim ten metres without stopping.
Swim twenty-five metres without stopping or touching the bottom.
Swim one hundred metres, then tread water for two minutes.
steps.note: Treading water means staying upright with your head out, not swimming. Two minutes is longer than it sounds.

steps.test: Swim in open water with an adult, with the safety done properly.

tracks.name: Cold water
tracks.line: Ankles to a proper dip.

steps.test: Stand in the sea up to your ankles for one minute.
how: Ankles only. Nothing brave required.
Breathe out slowly the whole first minute — that stops the gasp.
Dry feet and warm socks straight afterwards.

steps.test: Get in up to your waist and stay calm.
Get in up to your shoulders and control your breathing.
steps.note: The gasp is normal and passes in about ninety seconds. Breathe out long and slow and it goes.

steps.test: Stay in for two minutes and get warm again properly afterwards.
steps.note: Getting warm properly means dry clothes, something warm to drink and moving about — not a hot shower straight away.

steps.test: Do it once a week for a month, whatever the weather.
Take somebody else through their first cold dip safely.

tracks.name: Rowing and paddling
tracks.line: Getting in to crossing a lough.

steps.test: Get into a boat and sit safely without wobbling it.
Move a boat twenty metres under your own power.
steps.note: Under your own power means you moved it, not the wind or the current or somebody pushing.

steps.test: Steer around a marker and come back.
Paddle one kilometre.
Paddle five kilometres with a group.
Take a beginner out and bring them back confident.

tracks.name: Sailing
tracks.line: Naming the parts to sailing a course.

steps.test: Name the parts of a small boat and what each does.
Say which way the wind is coming from, without being told.
steps.note: Look at flags, smoke, or ripples on the water. The wind comes FROM the direction you name.

steps.test: Sail a straight line across the wind.
Tack, turn and come back to where you started.
Sail a full course with buoys.
Crew properly for somebody else and be useful.

tracks.name: Fishing
tracks.line: A rock pool to your own supper.

steps.test: Catch something in a rock pool with a net and put it back.
Set up a rod with a line and a hook, on your own.
steps.note: Rod, reel, line through the rings, then the hook. Barbless hooks are kinder and easier to get out.

steps.test: Cast and land the line where you meant it to go.
Catch a fish.
Catch, prepare and cook a fish you caught.
Teach somebody else to cast and land one.

tracks.name: Rock pools and shore
tracks.line: Five creatures to reading the shore.

steps.test: Find five different creatures in a rock pool.
steps.note: Look under the seaweed and on the underside of stones. Put every stone back the way it was.

steps.test: Name five of them correctly.
Explain what the tide does to everything living there.
Find and name ten seashore species.
Do a proper shore survey and write down what you found.
Lead a rock pool hunt for the younger children.

categories.name: Fitness and strength
categories.line: Press-ups, sit-ups, pull-ups, the plank, lifting, sprinting.

tracks.name: Press-ups
tracks.line: Two, up to fifty.

steps.test: Do two proper press-ups. Knees on the floor is fine.
how: Hands flat on the floor, a bit wider than your shoulders.
Knees down is completely fine — it is still a press-up.
Lower until your chest is a fist off the floor, then push back up.
Two of those. Slowly is easier than fast.

steps.test: Do five with your knees off the floor.
steps.note: Knees off the floor now. Chest to a fist above the ground and all the way back up, five times.

steps.test: Do ten in one go.
Do twenty-five in one go.
Do fifty in one go.
Do a hundred across one day, or get somebody else to their first one.

tracks.name: Sit-ups
tracks.line: Five, up to a hundred.

steps.test: Do five sit-ups.
how: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat on the floor.
Hands crossed on your chest so you cannot pull your own neck.
Curl up until your shoulders leave the floor, then lower back down.
Five of those.

steps.test: Do fifteen without stopping.
Do thirty without stopping.
Do fifty without stopping.
Do a hundred without stopping.
Do a hundred in under three minutes.

tracks.name: Pull-ups
tracks.line: Hanging on, up to ten.

steps.test: Hang from a bar with your feet off the ground for ten seconds.
how: Find a bar you can hang from with your feet clear of the ground.
Grip it with your hands about shoulder width, thumbs round.
Hang for ten seconds. Shoulders can relax — you are just hanging.

steps.test: Hang for a whole minute.
Do one pull-up from a dead hang, chin over the bar.
Do five in one go.
Do ten in one go.
Do fifteen, or help somebody else get their first one.

tracks.name: The plank
tracks.line: Twenty seconds, up to five minutes.

steps.test: Hold a plank for twenty seconds without your hips dropping.
how: Elbows under your shoulders, forearms flat on the floor.
Straight line from your head to your heels — no hips in the air, none sagging.
Twenty seconds. Squeeze your tummy the whole time.
steps.note: On your elbows, not your hands. A straight line from head to heels — a mirror or a photo will tell you.

steps.test: Hold it for one minute.
Hold it for two minutes.
Hold it for three minutes.
Hold it for five minutes.
Hold a side plank on each side for two minutes.

tracks.name: Squats
tracks.line: Ten, up to one on one leg.

steps.test: Do ten squats with your heels staying flat on the floor.
how: Feet about shoulder width, toes pointing slightly out.
Sit back as if there is a chair behind you, keeping your heels down.
Down until your thighs are level, then stand up. Ten of them.
steps.note: Heels flat is the whole thing. If they lift, you are not going as deep as you think.

steps.test: Do twenty-five in one go.
Do fifty in one go.
Do a hundred in one go.
Do twenty holding something heavy.
Do one squat on one leg, all the way down and back up.

tracks.name: Lifting
tracks.line: Picking it up right, to carrying a person.

steps.test: Pick something heavy up with your legs, back straight, and put it down again.
how: Stand close to it. Distance is what hurts backs.
Bend your knees, keep your back straight, and hold it against your body.
Push up with your legs. Put it down the same way.

steps.test: Carry something heavy fifty metres without putting it down.
Lift something as heavy as your own head off the ground overhead.
steps.note: Something about the weight of your own head is roughly four to five kilos — a bag of potatoes.

steps.test: Carry something half your own weight two hundred metres.
Carry your own bodyweight fifty metres.
Help somebody move house for a whole day and still be useful at the end.

tracks.name: Bending and stretching
tracks.line: Past your knees, to the splits.

steps.test: Reach past your knees with your legs straight.
how: Stand with your feet together and your legs straight.
Fold forward slowly from the hips and let your head hang heavy.
Get past your knees and hold for twenty seconds. Do not bounce.

steps.test: Touch your toes with your legs straight.
steps.note: Legs straight, no bouncing, and fingertips count. Warm muscles stretch further, so do it after moving.

steps.test: Hold your toes for thirty seconds without bending your knees.
Get your palms flat on the floor.
Sit on the floor with straight legs and hold your toes for a minute.
Do the splits, or a full backbridge.

tracks.name: Sprinting
tracks.line: Ten seconds flat out, to a real race.

steps.test: Sprint flat out for ten seconds.
how: Find twenty metres of clear grass or path.
Go absolutely flat out for ten seconds — properly, not jogging.
Walk back. Notice how you breathe afterwards.

steps.test: Run a hundred metres without slowing down at the end.
Time your hundred metres, then beat it.
steps.note: Get somebody to time you with a phone. Write it down, or you will not remember what you beat.

steps.test: Run a hundred metres in under twenty seconds.
Run a hundred metres in under sixteen seconds.
Win a race against somebody who beat you last time.

categories.name: Air and sky
categories.line: Kites, rockets, planes, stars, weather in the sky.

tracks.name: Kites
tracks.line: Flying one to making one that flies.

steps.test: Get a kite into the air and keep it there for a minute.
steps.note: Steady wind, back to it, and let the line out slowly. Running with it usually makes things worse.

steps.test: Launch and land it on your own, with no help.
Fly it for ten minutes without it coming down.
Make a kite from scratch that actually flies.
Make one that flies higher than a shop-bought one.
Teach two younger children to launch and land.

tracks.name: Rockets
tracks.line: A bottle rocket to a two-stage one.

steps.test: Make a paper rocket and launch it off a straw.
Make a water bottle rocket that leaves the ground.
steps.note: A two litre bottle, about a third full of water, pumped with a bike pump through a cork.

steps.test: Get one twenty metres up, measured.
Change one thing, test it, and say whether it helped.
steps.note: Change ONE thing — more water, less water, bigger fins — or you will not know what helped.

steps.test: Build one with a parachute that comes back down safely.
Run a rocket launch afternoon for the group.

tracks.name: Stars and planets
tracks.line: One constellation to knowing the sky.

steps.test: Find the Plough and the North Star.
steps.note: The Plough is seven bright stars like a saucepan. The two at the end of the pan point at the North Star.

steps.test: Name three constellations and find them on your own.
Find a planet with your own eyes and know which it is.
steps.note: Planets do not twinkle, stars do. Venus is the very bright one near sunrise or sunset.

steps.test: Know what the moon will look like tomorrow, and be right.
Watch a meteor shower and count what you see.
Run a stargazing night and show people what is up there.

tracks.name: Things that fly
tracks.line: Paper wings to something with a motor.

steps.test: Fold a paper aeroplane that flies across the room.
how: Fold an A4 sheet in half the long way, then open it out.
Fold the two top corners into the middle crease so you get a point.
Fold those long edges into the middle again, then fold the whole thing in half.
Fold a wing down on each side, and throw it level — not upwards.

steps.test: Fold one that flies ten metres, measured.
Fold one that flies thirty feet, measured, with witnesses.
Build a glider from balsa or card that flies properly.
steps.note: Balsa is light wood from a model shop. Card and a paper clip for weight at the nose also works.

steps.test: Build something with a motor or elastic that flies.
Build a small helicopter or drone that lifts and lands where you meant.

tracks.name: Wind and weather watching
tracks.line: Which way to keeping records.

steps.test: Say which way the wind is blowing without looking at anything.
Make something that shows wind direction and put it up.
Name five cloud types on sight.
steps.note: Cumulus, stratus, cirrus, cumulonimbus and a plain grey sheet will cover nearly every day here.

steps.test: Predict tomorrow from the sky alone and check if you were right.
Keep a weather record every day for a month.
Get five forecasts right in a row and explain how.

tracks.name: Throwing
tracks.line: Hitting a target to hitting it every time.

steps.test: Scrunch a sheet of paper into a ball and throw it into a bin from five paces.
how: Take any sheet of paper and scrunch it into a tight ball.
Stand five big paces back from a bin.
Throw underarm, not overarm — aim to drop it in from above rather than fire it.
Keep going until one goes in. It always does.

steps.test: Hit a target the size of a bin lid from ten paces.
Hit it five times out of five.
Skim a stone three bounces.
steps.note: Flat stone, low and hard, almost parallel to the water. Spin matters more than strength.

steps.test: Skim a stone six bounces.
Teach somebody else to skim one properly.

categories.name: Mind and numbers
categories.line: Tables, the cube, chess, memory, codes, puzzles.

tracks.name: Times tables
tracks.line: Counting in twos to sixty seconds flat.

steps.test: Count in twos up to twenty.
how: Two, four, six, eight, ten.
Keep going, adding two each time, all the way to twenty.
Say it out loud, not in your head.
Do it three times and it sticks.

steps.test: Say the two, five and ten times tables with no mistakes.
Say every table up to twelve correctly, no time limit.
steps.note: All of them means two up to twelve, in order, out loud, with nobody helping.

steps.test: Say every table up to twelve in under three minutes.
Say every table up to twelve in under ninety seconds.
Say every table up to twelve in under sixty seconds, and teach somebody theirs.

tracks.name: The cube
tracks.line: One face to under a minute.

steps.test: Name the pieces and turn the cube twenty times without losing which face is which.
how: A cube has centres, edges and corners. The centres never move.
Pick one face and keep your eye on its middle colour while you turn.
Turn it twenty times and still know which face was yours.

steps.test: Solve one whole face.
steps.note: One face means all nine squares the same colour. The layer underneath does not have to match yet.

steps.test: Solve the first two layers.
Solve the whole cube on your own, start to finish.
steps.note: There is a method with about seven steps to learn. Everybody looks it up — that is not cheating.

steps.test: Solve it in under two minutes.
Solve it in under sixty seconds.

tracks.name: Chess
tracks.line: Setting the board to teaching a beginner.

steps.test: Set the board up correctly and name every piece.
how: Board goes down with a white square in your bottom right corner.
Back row from the corner: rook, knight, bishop, then queen on her own colour, king beside her.
Pawns all along the row in front.

steps.test: Know how every piece moves, and play one full game to the end.
Win a game against somebody who is genuinely trying.
Checkmate with only a king and a rook.
steps.note: King and rook against a lone king. It is the ending everybody learns first and it always works.

steps.test: Beat an adult who plays properly.
Teach a complete beginner until they can play a full game.

tracks.name: Memory
tracks.line: Six digits to a hundred.

steps.test: Memorise a six-digit number and say it back a minute later.
how: Get somebody to write down any six digits.
Look for ten seconds. Say them out loud in a rhythm, like a phone number.
Do something else for a minute, then say them back.

steps.test: Memorise twenty objects in order and say them back an hour later.
steps.note: Get somebody to lay out twenty things while you look, then cover them. Making a silly story helps.

steps.test: Learn a twenty-line poem by heart.
Recite fifty digits of pi.
Memorise the order of a shuffled deck of cards.
steps.note: There is a proper method for this, and it is a picture for every card. Look it up.

steps.test: Recite one hundred digits of pi.

tracks.name: Mental arithmetic
tracks.line: Adding in your head to doing it fast.

steps.test: Add two single-digit numbers in your head, twenty in a row, correct.
Add two two-digit numbers in your head, five in a row.
Multiply a two-digit number by a single digit in your head.
steps.note: Break it up. Twenty-three times four is twenty times four, then three times four, added.

steps.test: Multiply two two-digit numbers in your head.
Work out a restaurant bill and the split, in your head, before anybody else.
Beat a calculator user on ten easy sums.

tracks.name: Codes and ciphers
tracks.line: A secret message to breaking one.

steps.test: Write a message in a shift cipher and have somebody read it.
steps.note: A shift cipher moves every letter the same number along. A becomes D if you shift by three.

steps.test: Crack a shift cipher you were not given the key to.
Invent your own cipher that a friend cannot break in ten minutes.
Use a book cipher or a keyword cipher properly.
Break a cipher using letter frequency.
steps.note: In English, E is the commonest letter, then T and A. Count the letters and the commonest is usually E.

steps.test: Run a treasure hunt for the group using codes.

tracks.name: Puzzles
tracks.line: A jigsaw to the hard stuff.

steps.test: Finish a twenty-four piece jigsaw on your own.
Finish a hundred-piece jigsaw on your own.
Finish an easy sudoku with no help.
Solve a wolf, goat and cabbage style riddle without being told.
steps.note: The classic: a wolf, a goat and a cabbage, one small boat, and you can only take one at a time.

steps.test: Finish a hard sudoku or a logic grid.
Write a puzzle of your own that stumps three people.

tracks.name: Finding things out
tracks.line: Asking well, looking it up, checking it.

steps.test: Ask somebody a question you do not know the answer to, and get an answer you understand.
how: Think of something you genuinely do not know. Not a test question — a real one.
Find a person who might know and ask them out loud.
If the answer does not make sense, say so and ask again. That bit is the skill.
You should be able to say it back in your own words afterwards.

steps.test: Look something up on your own and explain it back to another person.
Find out how to do something you have never done, then do it the same day.
Ask an AI a question so clear that the first answer it gives is actually useful.
steps.note: A good question says what you already know, what you want, and what a useful answer looks like.

steps.test: Check one fact in two different places and say which you trust more, and why.
steps.note: Two different places means two that did not copy each other. Say which you trust and why.

steps.test: Teach somebody else how you go about finding things out.

tracks.name: Maps
tracks.line: Finding yourself to drawing one.

steps.test: Find where you are standing on a paper map.
Point out three things on the map that you can see in real life.
Work out how far away something is using the map scale.
steps.note: The scale line at the edge tells you how far a centimetre is. Most walking maps are two and a half inches to the mile.

steps.test: Draw a map of your own area that somebody else can follow.
Read a timetable and plan a journey with a change in it.
Plan a whole day out for the group on paper, and then run it.

categories.name: Words and languages
categories.line: A new language, reading, handwriting, poems, stories, signing.

tracks.name: A new language
tracks.line: One sentence to a real conversation.

steps.test: Learn one usable sentence and say it out loud to another person.
how: Pick any language. Spanish, Irish, Polish, whichever.
Choose one sentence you would really use — 'where is the bread', 'my name is'.
Look up how it sounds and say it out loud ten times.
Say it to another person today. That is the whole level.
steps.note: Useful means you would actually say it. Not 'the cat is on the table'.

steps.test: Learn twenty words and use ten of them in a day.
Order food or ask directions in it, for real.
Hold a two-minute conversation without stopping.
steps.note: Two minutes without stopping. Getting it wrong and carrying on counts. Silence does not.

steps.test: Read a children's book in it, all the way through.
Have a proper conversation with somebody who grew up speaking it.

tracks.name: Irish
tracks.line: Your own name to a conversation.

steps.test: Say your own name and where you are from, in Irish.
Count to twenty and name ten everyday things.
Say five full sentences in a conversation.
Read a road sign or a placename and say what it means.
steps.note: Nearly every placename here means something — Bally is a town, Knock is a hill, Derry is an oak wood.

steps.test: Hold a two-minute conversation.
Tell a short story in Irish to the group.

tracks.name: Reading
tracks.line: Letter sounds to reading aloud to the little ones.

steps.test: Know the sound every letter makes.
how: Not the letter names — the sounds. B is 'buh', not 'bee'.
Go through the alphabet making the sound each letter makes.
Do it out loud with somebody who can tell you when it is off.
steps.note: The sound, not the name. B is 'buh'. Say it short — 'buh', not 'buhhh'.

steps.test: Read a short book out loud to somebody.
Read a chapter book on your own.
Read a book you chose yourself, all of it, because you wanted to.
Read something genuinely hard and explain it to somebody else.
steps.note: Genuinely hard means you had to stop and go back. Explaining it is how you find out if you got it.

steps.test: Read aloud to the younger children every week for a whole season.

tracks.name: Writing by hand
tracks.line: Your name to something that changes a mind.

steps.test: Write your own name so anybody could read it.
how: Capital letter first, then small ones.
Sit the letters on a line so they do not float.
Slowly. Neat beats fast every time.

steps.test: Write a sentence anybody can read.
Write a letter to a real person and post it.
Write a full page that stays readable to the last line.
steps.note: Readable to the last line is the test. Most people start neat and give up halfway down.

steps.test: Write a story of a thousand words that somebody finishes.
Write something that changes somebody's mind.

tracks.name: Beautiful writing
tracks.line: Neat to genuinely lovely.

steps.test: Write the alphabet neatly, all the same size.
Copy a line of italic or copperplate that looks like the example.
steps.note: Italic and copperplate are two styles you can print off a page and trace until it looks right.

steps.test: Write a whole quotation beautifully enough to put on a wall.
Write somebody's name as a gift.
Address and decorate an envelope somebody keeps.
Letter a sign or a poster the group actually uses.

tracks.name: Poems and lines
tracks.line: Four lines to running the evening.

steps.test: Learn a four-line rhyme and say it from memory.
how: Pick any four lines you like the sound of.
Say them out loud five times looking at the page.
Then cover it and say them again. Fill the gaps and repeat.

steps.test: Say eight lines from memory without a prompt.
Say twenty lines to the group, standing up.
steps.note: Standing up, from memory, loud enough for the back. Twenty lines is about a page.

steps.test: Learn a whole poem, forty lines or more.
Write your own and perform it.
Run a poetry evening for the group.

tracks.name: Sign language
tracks.line: The alphabet to a conversation.

steps.test: Finger-spell your own name.
steps.note: Irish Sign Language and British Sign Language have different alphabets. Pick one and stay with it.

steps.test: Learn twenty everyday signs.
Hold a one-minute conversation in signs.
Sign a whole song or a poem.
Have a real conversation with somebody who signs.
Teach the group ten signs they remember a week later.

categories.name: Speaking and people
categories.line: Strangers, the stage, listening, hard things, humour, teaching.

tracks.name: Talking to people you do not know
tracks.line: Hello, to interviewing anybody.

steps.test: Say hello and your name to a child you have never met.
how: Find somebody you have not met — at a day out, in a park, anywhere.
Walk up, look at their face, and say hello and your name.
That is it. You do not have to say anything after it.
If your voice goes odd, that is normal and it goes away by the fourth time.

steps.test: Ask somebody behind a counter a question, out loud, on your own.
Walk into a café, ask for a table and order your own food.
Interview an adult with ten questions you wrote yourself.
steps.note: Questions you wrote yourself, not ones somebody handed you. Write ten and use all ten.

steps.test: Interview somebody you have never met and get a real answer.
Teach another child to order their own meal, and stand back.

tracks.name: Standing up in front of people
tracks.line: The circle to the room.

steps.test: Say your name and one thing you like, at the welcome circle.
how: Wait until the circle is quiet.
Say your name, then one thing you like. Two sentences, that is all.
Look up at people rather than at the floor.

steps.test: Tell a story standing up, with your voice reaching the back.
Talk for two minutes about something you know, no notes.
steps.note: No notes at all. Two minutes is about three hundred words, which is less than it feels.

steps.test: Give a five-minute talk and take questions afterwards.
Speak to a room of fifty people.
Run the welcome circle at a day out.

tracks.name: Listening
tracks.line: Not interrupting, to coaching somebody.

steps.test: Listen to a whole story without needing to be the one talking.
Say back what somebody told you, in your own words, correctly.
steps.note: In your own words, not theirs. If they say 'yes, that is it', you did it.

steps.test: Ask three good follow-up questions and get somebody talking.
Listen to somebody much older for an hour, then tell somebody what you learned.
Help two people who are arguing sort it out, without taking a side.
Coach somebody through a problem without solving it for them.
steps.note: Coaching means asking questions until they see it. If you tell them the answer, it does not count.

tracks.name: Saying the hard thing
tracks.line: Sorry, no, and the truth, all kindly.

steps.test: Say sorry properly, and say what you will do instead.
Say no, out loud and kindly, when you mean no.
Disagree with somebody without either of you getting upset.
steps.note: Nobody upset means nobody raised their voice and nobody walked off. You can still disagree at the end.

steps.test: Tell a friend a hard truth, kindly, and stay friends.
Argue a case you personally disagree with, well.
Speak up for somebody who could not speak up for themselves.

tracks.name: Storytelling
tracks.line: One story to holding a room.

steps.test: Tell what happened today in the order it happened.
how: Think of one thing that actually happened today.
Tell it in the order it happened — first, then, then, and in the end.
Do not jump about. Order is the whole skill here.

steps.test: Tell a made-up story with a beginning, a middle and an end.
Tell a story that makes somebody laugh on purpose.
Tell one round a fire, from memory, that holds everybody.
steps.note: From memory, round a fire, holding everybody. If people talk over you, tell it again another night.

steps.test: Tell a story with different voices for each character.
Tell one to a room of thirty and hold them the whole way.

tracks.name: Being funny
tracks.line: One joke to your own material.

steps.test: Tell a joke well enough that somebody laughs.
Learn five jokes and land all five.
Make somebody laugh with something you thought of yourself.
Do two minutes of your own material to the group.
steps.note: Your own material means you wrote it. Two minutes is about six or seven attempts at a laugh.

steps.test: Do a sketch or an improv scene with somebody else.
Run a comedy night and keep it going.

tracks.name: Teaching
tracks.line: One thing to a whole session.

steps.test: Teach one person one thing you can do.
Teach it well enough that they can still do it a week later.
steps.note: A week later is the test, not on the day. Anybody can copy you while you are standing there.

steps.test: Teach three people at once.
Break something hard into steps and teach it in order.
Run a whole session for the younger children.
Teach an adult something they could not do before.

categories.name: Making and building
categories.line: Wood, cloth, clay, drawing, knots, electronics, machines, code.

tracks.name: Wood
tracks.line: Sanding to furniture.

steps.test: Sand a piece of wood properly smooth.
how: Always sand along the grain, never across it.
Start with rough paper, then finish with fine.
Run your hand over it with your eyes shut. Smooth is what you are after.

steps.test: Saw a straight cut you would be happy to show somebody.
steps.note: Straight means a pencil line drawn first and the cut following it. Let the saw do the work.

steps.test: Make something from two pieces joined together.
steps.note: Joined means glued, screwed or nailed and still together when you pick it up by one end.

steps.test: Draw a plan first, then build exactly that.
Build a piece of furniture somebody uses every day.
Teach a younger child to saw safely.

tracks.name: Cloth and thread
tracks.line: Threading a needle to clothes you would wear.

steps.test: Thread a needle on your own.
how: Cut the end of the thread clean at an angle — a fluffy end never goes in.
Wet the end between your lips and squash it flat.
Hold the needle against something light so you can see the hole.
Push the thread through and pull about ten centimetres out the other side.

steps.test: Sew a running stitch along a drawn line.
steps.note: In and out along a drawn line, stitches about the same size. Neat beats fast.

steps.test: Sew on a button that holds when it is pulled.
Mend a rip in something you would still wear out.
Sew a bag you would actually use.
Make a piece of clothing you would wear out of the house.

tracks.name: Knots and rope
tracks.line: One knot to a rope bridge.

steps.test: Tie a knot that does not come undone when pulled.
how: Take any rope or lace.
Tie a knot, then pull both ends as hard as you can.
If it holds and does not slip, that is the level.

steps.test: Tie a reef knot, a bowline and a clove hitch from memory.
steps.note: Reef for tying two ends together, bowline for a loop that will not slip, clove hitch for tying to a post.

steps.test: Lash two poles together so they hold your weight.
Whip or splice the end of a rope properly.
Build a structure from poles and lashings that holds a person.
Teach three knots to somebody until they can do them blind.

tracks.name: Clay and carving
tracks.line: A pinch pot to something on a shelf.

steps.test: Make a pinch pot that holds water.
steps.note: Push your thumb into a ball of clay and pinch the walls even. It has to hold water without leaking.

steps.test: Make something recognisable out of clay.
Carve a stick into a useful shape with a knife, safely.
Carve a spoon you would eat with.
Make a set of three things that match.
Make something somebody puts on a shelf and keeps.

tracks.name: Drawing
tracks.line: Recognisable, then good.

steps.test: Draw something and have somebody name it without being told.
how: Pick something in front of you — a cup, a shoe, a dog.
Look at the actual shape of it, not at the idea of it in your head.
Draw slowly. Nobody good draws fast.
Show it to somebody without telling them what it is.

steps.test: Draw from the thing in front of you rather than from your head.
steps.note: From life means the thing is in front of you while you draw. It always looks different to what is in your head.

steps.test: Draw the same thing five times and see it get better.
Draw a person in proportion.
steps.note: In proportion means the head is about a seventh of the height and the eyes are halfway down the head.

steps.test: Take three rounds of honest criticism and improve it each time.
Draw something somebody asks to keep.

tracks.name: Electricity
tracks.line: One bulb to your own circuit board.

steps.test: Light one bulb with a battery and two wires.
steps.note: Battery, wire to one side of the bulb, wire from the other side back to the battery. A complete loop.

steps.test: Build a circuit with a switch that works.
Build one where two things happen at once and explain why.
Solder a joint that holds and conducts.
steps.note: Soldering needs an adult beside you the first few times. Heat the joint, not the solder.

steps.test: Build something with a microcontroller that does a job.
Build something the group actually uses, and fix it when it breaks.

tracks.name: Machines and code
tracks.line: An idea out loud to something strangers use.

steps.test: Describe an idea for an app out loud in three clear sentences.
how: Think of something small you actually want.
Say it in three sentences: what it does, who uses it, what is on the screen.
Say it out loud to a person first. If they get it, an AI will.

steps.test: Get an AI to build something from your description that actually runs.
steps.note: Actually runs means you can open it and use it, not that it looked right in the answer.

steps.test: Fix what came back until it does what you meant.
Make something you genuinely use yourself.
Make something somebody else uses.
Put something you built out into the world for strangers.

tracks.name: Photography
tracks.line: A photo to an exhibition.

steps.test: Take a photo where you can tell what it is of.
Take one somebody asks for a copy of.
Take a photo of a person that looks like them.
Take twenty of one thing and pick the best three, and say why.
steps.note: Twenty of the same thing sounds mad and it is the whole exercise. You only see what is good by comparing.

steps.test: Print and frame one.
Put on a small exhibition of your own photographs.

categories.name: Music and voice
categories.line: Singing, an instrument, rhythm, songs, whistling, reading music.

tracks.name: Singing
tracks.line: A voice warm-up to singing in front of people.

steps.test: Do a voice warm-up every morning for one week.
how: Hum quietly up and down, low to high, five times.
Then sing 'me-may-mah-moh-moo' up a little each time.
Two minutes. Do it every morning for a week.
steps.note: Quietly is fine. A warm-up is humming and sliding up and down, not performing.

steps.test: Do a voice warm-up every morning for thirty days.
Sing one whole song in tune, on your own, to one person.
steps.note: In tune means somebody else could name the song. Sing it to one person, not a room.

steps.test: Sing a song to the group.
Sing a harmony line with somebody else.
Lead a song that everybody joins in with.

tracks.name: An instrument
tracks.line: One note to playing for people.

steps.test: Get one clear note out of an instrument.
Play a five-note tune anybody recognises.
steps.note: Any instrument. A tin whistle costs less than a takeaway and five notes gets you a tune.

steps.test: Play a whole tune from beginning to end.
Play three tunes from memory.
Play with somebody else, in time.
Play for the group at a day out.

tracks.name: Rhythm
tracks.line: Clapping in time to holding a beat for others.

steps.test: Clap in time with a song, all the way through.
how: Put on any song with a clear beat.
Clap on the beat — the bit you would nod your head to.
All the way to the end without losing it.

steps.test: Keep a steady beat on a drum for two minutes.
Clap a rhythm somebody gives you, back at them, correctly.
Play two different rhythms with your two hands.
steps.note: One hand steady, the other doing something different. It feels impossible for about a week.

steps.test: Hold the beat while other people play over it.
Lead a drum circle.

tracks.name: Whistling
tracks.line: One note to a whole tune.

steps.test: Whistle one clear note.
how: Wet your lips, then pull them into a small round hole.
Put the tip of your tongue low, behind your bottom teeth.
Blow gently — gently is the trick, hard never works.
Move your tongue back and forward until a note appears.

steps.test: Whistle up and down, high to low.
Whistle a tune somebody can name.
Whistle three tunes properly.
Whistle loudly with your fingers.
Teach somebody who cannot whistle to whistle.

tracks.name: Writing a song
tracks.line: Two lines to a song people sing.

steps.test: Write two lines that rhyme and mean something.
Write a whole verse.
Write a verse and a chorus and sing it to one person.
Write a whole song and perform it.
Write one for somebody, about them.
Write one the group sings without you starting it.

tracks.name: Reading music
tracks.line: Naming notes to sight-reading.

steps.test: Name every note on a line of written music.
steps.note: Every line and space is a letter from A to G. There are rhymes for remembering them.

steps.test: Clap the rhythm of a written line correctly.
Play a simple piece from the page, slowly.
Sight-read something you have never seen, slowly.
Write down a tune you heard, correctly.
Pass a graded music exam, or play a piece properly for the group.

tracks.name: Dance
tracks.line: One step to leading the floor.

steps.test: Learn one dance step and do it in time.
Learn a whole short dance and do it with somebody.
Dance a céilí dance properly with a set.
steps.note: A céilí dance is done in a set with other people. Somebody at any local class will show you.

steps.test: Learn a dance from another country.
Make up a dance and teach it to two people.
Lead the dancing at a group evening.

categories.name: Magic and performance
categories.line: Card tricks, coins, sleight of hand, mind reading, mime, puppets.

tracks.name: Card tricks
tracks.line: One trick to a whole act.

steps.test: Do one card trick that works, on one person.
steps.note: One trick, done once, that worked. A self-working one from a book counts.

steps.test: Shuffle a deck properly, twice, without dropping any.
Do a trick that genuinely fools an adult.
steps.note: Fools an adult means they cannot tell you how, not that they were polite about it.

steps.test: Do three tricks in a row without a mistake.
Do a trick with your own patter, in your own words.
Perform a five-minute card act for the group.

tracks.name: Coin tricks
tracks.line: Vanishing one to the whole routine.

steps.test: Make a coin vanish and reappear.
how: Hold a coin flat in your right fingers.
Pretend to take it with your left hand, but let it drop into your right palm.
Close the empty left hand and look at it. Everybody looks where you look.

steps.test: Do a French drop so nobody sees it.
Produce a coin from behind somebody's ear convincingly.
Do three coin moves in one routine.
Do it surrounded, with people watching from all sides.
Teach somebody the French drop until they can fool you.

tracks.name: Mind reading
tracks.line: One guess to a proper effect.

steps.test: Do a trick where you name a card somebody chose.
Do one that works on two people in a row.
Read somebody's body language and guess right three times.
steps.note: Body language is where they look, what their hands do, and whether they hesitate.

steps.test: Do a full mind reading effect with a story around it.
Do one where the method is invisible even on a second showing.
Perform three effects to the group and keep the method secret.

tracks.name: Mime and clowning
tracks.line: One gesture to holding a room silently.

steps.test: Mime one action so clearly that somebody names it.
how: Pick one everyday action — brushing teeth, opening a jar.
Do it slowly and make the invisible object the same size the whole way through.
Somebody has to name it without you saying a word.

steps.test: Do the invisible wall or the rope pull convincingly.
Tell a whole tiny story with no words.
Make somebody laugh without saying anything.
Perform a two-minute silent piece.
Run a mime game for the younger children.

tracks.name: Puppets
tracks.line: Making one to putting on a show.

steps.test: Make a puppet out of a sock or a paper bag.
Give it a voice and keep the voice the same for two minutes.
steps.note: The same voice for two minutes is harder than it sounds. Pick something easy to keep up.

steps.test: Make a puppet with moving parts.
Write and perform a short puppet story.
Build a stage and run a proper show.
Run a puppet show the younger children ask for again.

tracks.name: Circus skills
tracks.line: Spinning a plate to a routine.

steps.test: Spin a plate or a hoop and keep it going for thirty seconds.
Keep a diabolo or devil sticks going for thirty seconds.
Do ten keepy-uppies with a football.
Learn one trick with clubs, poi or a hoop.
steps.note: Poi are weights on cords, clubs are juggling pins, a hoop is a hula hoop. Any one of them.

steps.test: Put three circus tricks into one routine.
Perform your routine at a day out.

categories.name: Food and the kitchen
categories.line: Knife skills, cooking, baking, growing, preserving, hosting.

tracks.name: Knife and board
tracks.line: Buttering bread to teaching a younger one.

steps.test: Butter a slice of bread properly.
how: Take the butter out early so it is soft. Cold butter tears bread.
Hold the bread flat on a board, not in your hand.
Spread from the middle outwards, right to the edges.
All the way to the corners is the level.

steps.test: Peel a vegetable without taking half of it away.
Chop safely, sitting down, with an adult beside you.
steps.note: Sitting down, board flat, fingers curled back like a claw. Slow is safe.

steps.test: Prepare all the vegetables for a whole meal.
Joint a chicken or fillet a fish.
steps.note: Jointing means taking a chicken into pieces at the joints. There are videos and it is easier than it looks.

steps.test: Teach a younger child to chop safely.

tracks.name: Cooking a meal
tracks.line: Cold breakfast to feeding the group.

steps.test: Make yourself a cold breakfast and clear it away.
how: Cereal and milk, or toast and fruit. Cold is fine.
Get everything out first, make it, then eat it.
Clearing your own plate away is part of the level.

steps.test: Make a hot drink safely.
Cook a hot meal for yourself.
steps.note: Hot and made by you, start to finish, including getting things out and putting them away.

steps.test: Cook a hot meal for your family.
Cook three courses and get them on the table hot.
Cook for the whole group at a day out.

tracks.name: Baking
tracks.line: Weighing to selling.

steps.test: Weigh ingredients accurately on a scale.
steps.note: Accurate means to the gram on a digital scale. Baking is the one place where guessing shows.

steps.test: Bake something by following a recipe on your own.
Make a loaf of bread from flour and water.
steps.note: Flour, water, salt and yeast. Time does most of the work — that is why bread is a good first thing.

steps.test: Bake something without looking at the recipe.
Bake to order for somebody else, to what they asked for.
Sell what you baked to people who are not related to you.

tracks.name: Cooking on fire
tracks.line: Toast on a stick to a whole meal outdoors.

steps.test: Toast something on a stick over a fire and eat it.
Cook an egg or a sausage over a fire without burning it.
Bake bread twist on a stick.
Cook a one-pot meal over a fire for two people.
Cook a full meal outdoors for six.
Run the fire and the food for a whole day out.

tracks.name: Growing
tracks.line: One seed to feeding people.

steps.test: Plant a seed and keep it alive for a month.
how: A bean or a sunflower seed in a pot of compost, one knuckle deep.
On a windowsill with light. Water when the top feels dry, not every day.
Alive in a month is the level.

steps.test: Grow something you then eat.
steps.note: Radishes are about four weeks, salad leaves about five. Both work in a pot on a windowsill.

steps.test: Grow three different things through a whole season.
Save seed and grow next year's from it.
Grow enough to give some away.
Run a growing patch for the group.

tracks.name: Keeping food
tracks.line: Jam to a full store cupboard.

steps.test: Make jam that sets.
steps.note: Sets means it wrinkles when you push it on a cold plate. Under-set jam is a sauce, which is fine too.

steps.test: Pickle something and eat it a month later.
Dry or freeze a harvest properly.
Bake with something you preserved yourself.
Fill a shelf with things you made that keep.
Give away a box of it and have people ask for more.

tracks.name: Feeding people
tracks.line: Laying a table to hosting an evening.

steps.test: Lay a table properly for everybody.
steps.note: Properly means everybody has what they need to eat with before anybody has to ask.

steps.test: Serve a meal and make sure everybody has what they need.
Plan a meal for six on paper before cooking it.
Cook and host a meal for people who are not family.
Do it to a budget and come in under.
Host an evening people ask you to do again.

categories.name: Money and business
categories.line: Handling it, earning it, selling, running something, investing.

tracks.name: Handling money
tracks.line: Naming coins to a weekly shop.

steps.test: Name every coin and note when somebody holds one up.
how: Get somebody to lay out all the coins and notes.
Name each one, then shut your eyes and name three by feel.
The two-pound and the ten-pence catch everybody out.

steps.test: Count out one pound in three different ways.
Pay for something yourself and check the change is right.
Give correct change from a five-pound note, five times running.
steps.note: Five times running with no mistakes. Count it back into their hand out loud.

steps.test: Keep a written record of money in and out for a month, and balance it.
Do a full weekly shop to a budget and come in under it.

tracks.name: Earning
tracks.line: One job to paying somebody else.

steps.test: Do one real job and be paid for it.
Do a job for somebody outside your own family.
Hold a paid job around the place for a season, and turn up for it.
Save half of everything you earn for a month.
Turn ten pounds into thirty pounds honestly, and show your working.
steps.note: Honestly means you made something or did something, not that somebody gave it to you.

steps.test: Pay another person a fair share for their part in something you ran.

tracks.name: Selling
tracks.line: One thing to one person, to a real product.

steps.test: Sell one thing to one person.
Run a stall with real money and real change.
Sell to ten people you have never met.
Price something so it sells, and defend the price when asked.
steps.note: Defending the price means saying what it cost you and why it is worth it, without apologising.

steps.test: Handle somebody being unhappy with what you sold, and put it right.
Make something strangers buy more than once.

tracks.name: Running something
tracks.line: A plan on paper to being asked back.

steps.test: Write down on paper what a small event would need.
Run one part of an outing yourself.
Organise a small event for the group and make it happen.
Make an event cover its own costs with nobody topping it up.
steps.note: Covering its costs means the money in is at least the money out. Write both down before you start.

steps.test: Find out what people actually want first, then do that.
Run something people ask you to do again.

tracks.name: Making money grow
tracks.line: Saving to understanding it.

steps.test: Save for four weeks without spending any of it.
Explain what interest is, in your own words, correctly.
steps.note: Interest is money paid for the use of money. Try explaining it with a real example, not a definition.

steps.test: Buy something, improve it, and sell it for more.
Explain what a share in a company actually is.
Track a small investment for six months and explain what happened.
Teach a younger child what saving and interest mean.

tracks.name: Negotiating
tracks.line: Asking to a fair deal.

steps.test: Ask for something you want, out loud, in a full sentence.
Swap something with somebody so you are both pleased.
Ask for a better price and get one.
steps.note: Ask politely and be willing to hear no. Markets, car boot sales and second-hand things are the places to try.

steps.test: Walk away from a deal that was not good enough.
Sort out a disagreement where both sides end up content.
Negotiate something real on behalf of somebody else.

categories.name: Beauty and buildings
categories.line: Why one street feels good and another does not. Shapes, proportion, arches, and your own town.

tracks.name: Looking at buildings
tracks.line: Noticing, then being able to say why.

steps.test: Point at a building you think is pretty and one you think is ugly, and say which is which.
how: Stand somewhere you can see several buildings at once.
Point at the one you would most like to look at every day.
Then point at the one you would least like to look at.
Say which is which out loud. That is the whole level — you do not have to justify it yet.

steps.test: Say one reason why. Any reason counts, including a feeling.
steps.note: A feeling is a real reason. 'It looks friendly' or 'the windows are all different sizes' both count.

steps.test: Find two buildings on the same street and say which you would rather live in, and why.
Photograph three you like and three you do not, then find one thing the good ones share.
steps.note: Look for the things they share rather than the things you like. Often it is even windows, a proper roof, or that the door is where you expect.

steps.test: Walk somebody round and show them the good and the bad, and have them see it too.
Write down, in your own words, five rules for what makes a building good.

tracks.name: Proportion
tracks.line: Why some shapes feel right and others do not.

steps.test: Fold a piece of string exactly in half by eye, then check it.
how: Cut a piece of string about as long as your arm.
Fold it where you THINK the middle is. Do not measure first.
Now bring the two ends together and see how close you were.
Do it three times. You get better at it very quickly, and that is the point.

steps.test: Look at two rectangles and say which one feels nicer to you. There is no wrong answer.
steps.note: There genuinely is no wrong answer. Most people pick a rectangle roughly half again as long as it is wide, and nobody knows why.

steps.test: Draw a house and put the door at a size that looks right for a person.
steps.note: A door is about twice as tall as it is wide, and a person is about three doors tall on a normal house.

steps.test: Divide a line into three equal parts by eye, then measure and see how close you got.
Find something around you about one and a half times as long as it is wide, and prove it with a ruler.
steps.note: About one and a half to one. A bank card, a book, a window — measure the long side and the short side and divide.

steps.test: Draw the front of a building where every part looks right beside every other part.

tracks.name: Shapes and geometry
tracks.line: Circles, squares, tiles and solids.

steps.test: Find a circle, a square and a triangle in the room you are in.
how: Look around the room you are in right now.
A circle: a plate, a clock, a door handle. A square: a tile, a window, a book.
A triangle is the hard one — try a roof, a coat hanger, a slice of something.
Point at each and name it.

steps.test: Draw a circle freehand that somebody else agrees is properly round.
Draw a square and check its corners against the corner of a page.
Make a shape that tiles, and fit six of them together with no gaps.
steps.note: Squares, triangles and hexagons tile on their own. Circles never do, which is why floors are not made of them.

steps.test: Step a compass around a circle six times and have it close exactly on itself.
steps.note: Keep the compass exactly the same width the whole way round. If it closes on itself, you have drawn a hexagon.

steps.test: Cut and fold paper into a solid shape — a cube, or a pyramid that stands up.

tracks.name: Symmetry and pattern
tracks.line: Repeats, mirrors, and why they calm a room.

steps.test: Fold paper, cut a shape, open it out, and see the two halves match.
how: Fold a sheet of paper in half and press the crease flat.
Cut a shape out of the FOLDED edge — do not cut the fold away completely.
Open it out. Whatever you cut on one side has appeared on the other.
That is symmetry, and you just made some.

steps.test: Find three symmetrical things around you.
Make a pattern that repeats six times without a mistake.
Draw the missing half of a face or a building so both sides match.
Find a symmetrical building and a lopsided one, and say which feels calmer to stand in front of.
steps.note: Most old public buildings are symmetrical and most modern ones are not. Notice which one your eye settles on.

steps.test: Design a tile that still works when you repeat it in every direction.

tracks.name: Arches and columns
tracks.line: The old ways, and why they were used.

steps.test: Find an arch somewhere near you and stand underneath it.
how: Arches are over doorways, under bridges, in old churches and railway stations.
Find one and go and stand underneath it.
Look up. Notice the stones or bricks are wedge shaped and lean on each other.

steps.test: Build an arch out of blocks that stands up on its own.
steps.note: Build the two sides up leaning inwards, and the last stone at the very top is the one that locks it. Bricks or wooden blocks both work.

steps.test: Point out the three parts of a column — the base, the shaft and the top.
steps.note: The base is what it stands on, the shaft is the tall part, the top is called the capital.

steps.test: Say in your own words why an arch holds more weight than a flat beam.
steps.note: An arch pushes the weight sideways into the walls instead of hanging it in the middle, which is where a flat beam breaks.

steps.test: Find a column, an arch and a dome all in one day.
Explain to somebody younger why old buildings were built this way.

tracks.name: Your own town
tracks.line: Reading the place you actually live.

steps.test: Walk down your street and count the buildings you like.
how: Walk the length of one street, slowly, looking up rather than ahead.
Count the buildings you actually like the look of.
Say the number out loud at the end. Most people are surprised how low it is.

steps.test: Find the oldest building near you and say what is different about it.
steps.note: Older usually means smaller windows, thicker walls, more stone, and more bother taken over the bits near the door.

steps.test: Draw a map of one street with the good buildings marked on it.
Find a spot in your town that feels good to stand in, and say what makes it so.
steps.note: Places that feel good are often enclosed but not closed in — something to look at, somewhere to sit, and not too much noise.

steps.test: Find a spot that feels bad to stand in, and say what would fix it.
Take somebody round and show them the town the way you now see it.

categories.name: The classical mind
categories.line: Logic, the big questions, the great stories, and one beautiful thing a day.

tracks.name: Spotting a bad argument
tracks.line: Telling a good argument from a loud one.

steps.test: Notice somebody changing the subject instead of answering, and say so afterwards.
how: Listen for it in a real conversation, not in a book.
Somebody asks a question, and the answer is about something else entirely.
Do not interrupt. Afterwards, say to somebody what actually happened.
Once you have heard it once you will hear it constantly.

steps.test: Say what is wrong with 'everybody does it, so it must be fine'.
steps.note: Lots of people doing a thing does not make it right, and never did. That is all you need to say.

steps.test: Spot three different bad arguments in a week and write down what was wrong with each.
Name five kinds of bad argument and give a real example of each.
steps.note: Attacking the person instead of the point, either-or when there are more options, everybody-does-it, one story treated as proof, and slippery slopes.

steps.test: Point one out kindly, in the moment, without making anybody feel small.
Teach somebody younger how to tell a good argument from a loud one.

tracks.name: Asking the good question
tracks.line: The Socratic habit, at any age.

steps.test: Ask why three times in a row about the same thing and see where you end up.
how: Pick anything. Why is the sky blue, why do we go to bed, why is that rule there.
Whatever answer you get, ask why again.
Then once more. Three deep is usually where it gets interesting.
Ask kindly, not to catch anybody out.

steps.test: Ask somebody what a word really means, and keep going until it is clear.
Take a word like fair or brave and give an example and a non-example.
Ask questions for five whole minutes without giving your own opinion once.
Change your own mind out loud, because of an answer somebody gave you.
Run a question with a group and keep everybody talking.

tracks.name: The big questions
tracks.line: Philosophy, done out loud, from about five upwards.

steps.test: Say what you think the word good means, in your own words.
how: Not the dictionary meaning — what YOU think it means.
Try finishing this: something is good when...
Give an example of something good and something not good, and see if your rule fits both.
There is no right answer here and that is the point.

steps.test: Answer this and give a reason: is it ever right to tell a lie?
If every plank of a ship is replaced one by one, is it still the same ship? Say why.
steps.note: It is called the Ship of Theseus and adults have argued about it for two thousand years. There is no answer, only better reasons.

steps.test: Argue properly for the opposite of what you actually believe.
Read a page of a philosopher and say one thing you agreed with and one you did not.
Run a proper discussion for the group and let the best answer win, even if it is not yours.

tracks.name: The great stories
tracks.line: Myths, fables, and the books people keep reading.

steps.test: Listen to a whole myth or fable and say what happened.
Say what the story was actually about, underneath the events.
Tell one from memory to somebody else.
Read a whole book that people have been reading for hundreds of years.
steps.note: Homer, the Odyssey, Aesop, the Norse or Irish myths, Robinson Crusoe, Treasure Island. Old enough that your grandparents' grandparents read it.

steps.test: Find the same idea turning up in two different old stories.
Read one aloud to the younger ones, doing the voices.

tracks.name: Words and where they come from
tracks.line: Latin and Greek, the useful way.

steps.test: Learn what one word root means and find two English words that use it.
how: Try 'aqua', which means water. Aquarium. Aqueduct.
Or 'photo', which means light. Photograph. Photosynthesis.
Pick one, learn what it means, and find two English words built on it.

steps.test: Learn ten roots and what they mean.
Work out a long word you have never seen before, from its parts alone.
steps.note: Break it into pieces first. Tele means far, scope means to look. Bio means life, logy means the study of.

steps.test: Learn twenty Latin or Greek words and use them correctly.
Read one line of Latin or Greek and say what it means.
Teach somebody to break a long word into its parts.

tracks.name: One beautiful thing a day
tracks.line: Looking on purpose, and keeping what is worth keeping.

steps.test: Find one beautiful thing today and say why it is.
how: It can be anything — a tree, a chair, a bit of sky, a face, a sound.
Stop and look at it properly for ten seconds rather than glancing.
Then say out loud what makes it beautiful. Trying to say it is most of the exercise.

steps.test: Do it every day for a week.
Do it every day for a month and write each one down.
Keep a commonplace book for a month — copy in anything worth keeping.
steps.note: A commonplace book is just a notebook where you copy anything worth keeping — a line, a fact, a bit of a poem. People have kept them for centuries.

steps.test: Learn one piece of music, one poem or one painting well enough to describe it from memory.
Show somebody something beautiful they had been walking past for years.

tracks.name: Thinking on your own
tracks.line: A walk, a question, and no screen.

steps.test: Walk or sit for ten minutes with nothing to look at, thinking about one thing.
how: No phone, no book, no music, nobody talking to you.
Walk, or sit somewhere you can see out.
Pick one question before you start and stay with it for ten minutes.
Boredom for the first two minutes is normal. Go past it.
steps.note: This is genuinely hard the first time and gets easy fast. Ten minutes without input is where most of your own ideas live.

steps.test: Say afterwards what you worked out.
Write down what you actually think about something, a page of it.
Do that every week for a month.
Change your mind on paper, and write down what changed it.
Keep it going for a whole season.

categories.name: Nerve
categories.line: Small brave things, done on purpose, until they stop being brave. The later levels are for older ones and adults.

tracks.name: Asking out loud
tracks.line: From the time of day to the thing you actually want.

steps.test: Ask a stranger the time, or for directions you do not really need.
how: Pick somebody who does not look busy.
Make eye contact first, then ask. Excuse me, do you have the time?
Say thank you and walk on. That is the whole thing.
It takes about eight seconds and it is the doorway to all the rest.

steps.test: Ask for something small in a shop — a bag, a glass of water, what they would recommend.
Ask politely for a discount, and take no cheerfully.
steps.note: Ask once, pleasantly, and mean it. If it is no, say thanks anyway and be genuinely fine about it — that part is the skill.

steps.test: Ask somebody for a favour you would normally talk yourself out of asking for.
Ask for something you genuinely want, from somebody who could actually say yes.
Take somebody else out and get them to do their first ask.

tracks.name: Walking in
tracks.line: Rooms where you know nobody.

steps.test: Walk into a room where you know nobody, and stay.
how: A class, a club, a talk, a group at a day out — anywhere you know nobody.
Go in and stay at least twenty minutes. Leaving early is the thing to beat.
You do not have to talk to anybody the first time. Staying is the level.

steps.test: Join a class or a group where everybody already knows each other.
Sit down with people you have never met and start a conversation.
steps.note: Ask whatever you actually want to know. Looking at things is what a shop is for, and staff are there to be asked.

steps.test: Turn up to something on your own, having told nobody you were coming.
steps.note: You are not obliged to buy anything and you do not owe anybody an explanation. You are deciding whether you like it, which is exactly what a customer does. Behave like one, ask your questions, and leave when you have your answer.

steps.test: Go to something where you are the only one of your kind in the room.
Bring somebody who would never have gone on their own.

tracks.name: On the phone
tracks.line: The call you would rather send a message about.

steps.test: Make one phone call you would rather have sent a message about.
how: Pick the one that has been sitting on your list.
Write down the one sentence you need to say, then dial before you reread it.
It is nearly always shorter and easier than the version in your head.

steps.test: Phone a shop and ask whether they have something.
Phone somewhere expensive and ask real questions about what they do.
steps.note: Ask what you want to know the way any caller would. You do not have to hand over your life story or your details to find out what something costs.

steps.test: Phone to sort out something that went wrong, politely, and get it put right.
Phone a stranger to ask for information, advice or an introduction.
Make five calls in one day that you had been putting off.

tracks.name: Getting told no
tracks.line: Collecting refusals until they stop stinging.

steps.test: Ask for something you are fairly sure will be refused, and be refused.
how: Ask for something small and unreasonable but harmless — a free coffee, a look behind the counter.
Be pleasant. You are not trying to trick anybody.
When they say no, smile, say no problem, and go. The no is the point, not the thing.
steps.note: This is sometimes called rejection practice. The aim is to find out that a no costs you nothing at all.

steps.test: Collect three noes in a week, on purpose.
Collect ten noes, and notice that nothing bad happened.
Ask one more question after a no, instead of walking off.
Turn a no into a yes by asking a different way.
steps.note: Usually it is asking for something smaller, asking a different person, or simply explaining why you are asking.

steps.test: Take somebody else out collecting noes.

tracks.name: Speaking up on the spot
tracks.line: No warning, no notes.

steps.test: Say something out loud in a group of people you do not know.
how: A queue, a class, a waiting room, a group at a day out.
One sentence out loud that other people can hear. A question is easiest.
Your heart will go faster than the situation deserves. That is the muscle working.

steps.test: Ask a question at a talk or an event, in front of everybody.
Stand up and thank somebody publicly, in a room.
Speak for two minutes with no warning at all.
Speak up when something is wrong and nobody else has.
Take a microphone you were not expecting to be handed.

tracks.name: Not minding what people think
tracks.line: Harmless, cheerful, and entirely your own business.

steps.test: Wear something you would normally think twice about, for a whole day.
how: A bright coat, an odd hat, colours you would not usually put together.
Wear it all day, including where people know you.
Count how many people actually say anything. It is almost always nobody.

steps.test: Hum or sing out loud somewhere people can hear you.
Dance where people can see you.
Sit alone in a café for an hour with no phone out.
steps.note: An hour is longer than it sounds. Bring nothing. Watch the room, think, or do nothing at all.

steps.test: Do something harmlessly odd in public and stay for the reaction.
steps.note: Harmless is the whole rule. Nobody inconvenienced, nobody frightened, nothing damaged, and stop the moment it stops being cheerful.

steps.test: Do the thing you have been putting off purely because of what people would think.

categories.name: Negotiation
categories.line: Almost everything is flexible — the price, the terms, the timing. Most people simply never ask.

tracks.name: Asking for a better price
tracks.line: From asking at home to shifting a printed price tag.

steps.test: Ask somebody at home for something you want, and give one good reason why they should say yes.
how: Pick something you actually want — later bedtime, a lift somewhere, a thing you would like.
Ask plainly, then give ONE reason why it is a good idea for them, not just for you.
Then stop talking and let them answer. The silence is the hard part.
That is a negotiation. You have just done one.

steps.test: Find out what somebody else pays for something you pay for — a phone, a haircut, a subscription.
Ask for a discount in a shop or at a market, out loud, once.
steps.note: Say it plainly and pleasantly: is there any movement on the price? Then stop talking. Markets, independent shops and anything second-hand are the easiest places to start.

steps.test: Get three different prices for the same thing before you buy anything.
Get money off by asking, then write down the exact words that worked.
Get a better price on something that had a printed price tag on it.
steps.note: A printed price feels fixed and mostly is not — especially on the last one, a display model, something marked, or when you are buying more than one.

tracks.name: Asking for more instead of less
tracks.line: Value is easier to move than price.

steps.test: Ask for something extra that costs them nothing — a bag, more sauce, a longer look.
how: Anywhere that serves you — a café, a shop, a takeaway.
Ask for something small that costs them nothing at all.
Ask pleasantly and as if it is completely normal, because it is.
Notice how often the answer is simply yes.

steps.test: Ask for a free upgrade somewhere, pleasantly, and take no cheerfully.
Get something added in for nothing — delivery, a case, an extra portion, a longer guarantee.
When the price will not move, ask what else they can do instead.
steps.note: This is the most useful question in the whole category. If the price is fixed, the extras usually are not.

steps.test: Get an upgrade on something that actually mattered — a seat, a room, a service.
