Show somebody else that asking for more is easier than asking for less.

tracks.name: From your chair
tracks.line: The bills you have never once questioned.

steps.test: Find one thing your household pays every month and work out what it costs in a year.
how: Phone, streaming, insurance, broadband, a gym, a subscription.
Find the monthly amount and multiply it by twelve.
Write that yearly number down and look at it. Most people have never seen it.

steps.test: Look up what a brand new customer pays for that same thing.
Phone them and ask, plainly, whether that is the best they can do.
steps.note: Ask for what any customer would ask for. You do not owe them a reason and you do not have to threaten to leave.

steps.test: Ask to be put through to somebody who can actually change it.
steps.note: The first person you speak to often cannot change anything. Retentions, customer loyalty or a supervisor usually can.

steps.test: Get a rate, a fee or a bill reduced by asking for it.
Go through every regular bill you have in one afternoon.

tracks.name: Terms, not just the price
tracks.line: The price is often the least flexible part.

steps.test: Write down three things about something you are buying that are not the price.
how: Think of anything you are about to buy, big or small.
Write down three things that matter besides the price — when it arrives, how long it is guaranteed, whether you can send it back.
Those three are usually easier to move than the price is.

steps.test: Ask when it could arrive, and whether sooner is possible.
Ask for longer to pay, or to pay in parts.
Ask for a better guarantee or a longer window to change your mind.
Improve a deal without the price changing at all.
Explain to somebody why the price is usually the last thing to move.

tracks.name: Being willing to walk away
tracks.line: The quietest strength there is.

steps.test: Before you go, write down the number you will not go above.
how: Decide the number BEFORE you are standing in front of the thing.
Write it on your hand or on your phone.
A number decided in advance is worth ten decided on the spot.

steps.test: Leave something in a shop that you wanted, because it was not right.
steps.note: You have not lost anything. Wanting something is not the same as needing it today.

steps.test: Say out loud 'that is more than I want to spend', and then stop talking.
Walk away from a deal, and be glad about it afterwards.
Have somebody come back to you with a better offer after you left.
Walk away from something you really wanted, because the terms were wrong.

tracks.name: Both sides pleased
tracks.line: The deals people come back for.

steps.test: Swap something with somebody so that you are both happy.
Ask somebody what they actually need before you say what you want.
steps.note: People will tell you what they need if you ask. It is very often not the thing you assumed.

steps.test: Do a deal where the other person clearly got something they wanted too.
Settle a disagreement so both people came away with most of it.
Do a deal that somebody thanks you for afterwards.
Become somebody people want to deal with again.

categories.name: You belong here
categories.line: Fine shops, grand rooms and expensive things — so you never again decide somewhere is above you.

tracks.name: From where you are sitting
tracks.line: All of this can start today, at home.

steps.test: Look up a grand building near you that is open to the public, and find its opening times.
how: Try the city hall, the courthouse, a cathedral, a university, a museum, a big old library.
Search the name plus 'opening times' or 'visitors'.
Most of them are open to anybody and free, and almost nobody knows it.
You are not going today. You are just finding out that you could.

steps.test: Look up the real price of something you would never normally price — a watch, a car, a suite.
Phone a dealership and ask two questions about a model. Two minutes, then thank them and go.
steps.note: Ask two real questions — what engine, what it costs, when it is available. Two minutes, thank them, done. You are not committing to anything by asking.

steps.test: Phone a fine hotel and ask what is included in a room.
Contact somewhere you assume would never reply, and ask something real.
Book something in advance that you would normally have talked yourself out of.

tracks.name: Fine shops
tracks.line: Looking properly, and being helped.

steps.test: Walk into an expensive shop and look at three things properly, without hurrying.
how: Somewhere you would normally walk past because of the prices in the window.
Go in, and look at three things properly — pick them up if they can be picked up.
Nobody is going to ask you to leave. Looking is what the shop is for.
Leave when you are finished, not when you start feeling awkward.

steps.test: Let an assistant come over, and tell them what you are looking at.
Ask to try something on — a watch, a coat, a jacket.
steps.note: Trying something on is normal and expected, and it is what the mirror is there for. Nobody is keeping score.

steps.test: Try on something far beyond what you would ever spend, and look in the mirror.
Spend half an hour somewhere expensive without buying and without apologising.
Take somebody who would never have gone in on their own.

tracks.name: Cars
tracks.line: Sitting in it is free.

steps.test: Look up a car you like and read what it actually costs.
how: Pick a car you have always liked the look of.
Find the real price, and the monthly figure if it is leased.
Knowing the actual number takes most of the mystery out of it.

steps.test: Walk into a dealership and look at one car, unhurried.
Sit in it, adjust the seat, and stay there a few minutes.
steps.note: Ask if you may sit in it and they will nearly always say yes. Take your time. Adjust the seat. It is allowed.

steps.test: Ask the questions you actually want answered.
Take a test drive.
Take somebody else for their first look.

tracks.name: Grand rooms
tracks.line: Most of them are open, and most people never check.

steps.test: Find out which grand buildings near you are open to the public.
steps.note: City halls, courthouses, cathedrals, university buildings, old libraries and many galleries are open to anybody and free. Almost nobody realises.

steps.test: Walk into a fine hotel lobby and sit down for ten minutes.
Visit the city hall, the courthouse, a gallery or a cathedral, and look up.
Have a coffee or afternoon tea somewhere far smarter than you would normally.
Go to an event in a building you had assumed was not for you.
Eat alone in a good restaurant, with no phone on the table.
steps.note: No phone, no book. Just you, the food, and the room. It is far easier than people expect and it changes something.

tracks.name: Carrying yourself
tracks.line: Not shrinking is a physical habit.

steps.test: Walk into a room with your head up and make eye contact with one person.
how: Head up, shoulders back, and slow down rather than speed up.
Find one person and meet their eyes for about a second.
That is it. It is a physical habit and it rewires surprisingly fast.

steps.test: Take up your full space — do not shrink, and do not hurry through.
Let somebody serve you without apologising for the trouble.
steps.note: Sorry-for-the-trouble is a habit, not manners. Thank you does the same job without shrinking.

steps.test: Take a compliment with a thank you, and nothing after it.
Ask for what you want in a room where you feel out of place.
Notice that you have stopped feeling out of place, and say when it changed.

tracks.name: The story you tell yourself
tracks.line: Testing the thing you assume would happen.

steps.test: Write down one place you avoid because you have decided it is not for you.
how: Be honest and be specific. Not 'posh places' but the actual shop, street or building.
One is enough to start with.
Keep the paper. You are going to check it against what actually happens.

steps.test: Write down what you assume would happen there. Keep the paper.
Notice one time you talked yourself out of something, and write down the exact thought.
Go to the place, and compare what happened with what you wrote.
steps.note: Read what you wrote before you went, then write what actually happened. The gap between the two is the whole point of this track.

steps.test: Go somewhere every week for a month that you used to avoid.
Tell somebody the story you used to believe, and what actually happened instead.

categories.name: Home and repair
categories.line: Keeping a place, mending, tools, bikes, first aid, engines.

tracks.name: Keeping a place
tracks.line: Your own things to the whole house.

steps.test: Put your own things away without being asked twice.
how: Look round the room for the things that are yours.
Put each one back where it actually lives, not on a pile.
Do it without anybody asking you twice.

steps.test: Sweep a floor and get the whole pile into the bin.
Wash up a full sink and put everything back where it lives.
Clean a room properly enough that it passes a close look.
steps.note: A close look means somebody else checks the corners, the skirting and behind the door.

steps.test: Do a load of washing from the basket to folded and put away.
Look after the house for a whole day — food, tidy, animals, all of it.

tracks.name: Mending
tracks.line: A screw to fixing things for other people.

steps.test: Tighten a loose screw with the right screwdriver.
how: Find a screw that is loose — a door handle, a chair, a hinge.
Match the screwdriver to the screw head. The wrong one chews it up.
Push in hard while you turn. Most of the work is pushing, not turning.
Turn clockwise until it is snug, then stop.

steps.test: Glue something so it stays fixed a month later.
Sew or patch something back into use.
steps.note: Take the tube out, find the hole in water, patch it, and it should hold overnight.

steps.test: Fix something rather than replacing it, three times.
Put up a shelf that is level and holds weight.
Fix something for somebody else who could not.

tracks.name: Tools
tracks.line: Naming them to teaching safety.

steps.test: Name ten tools and say what each one is for.
how: Open the toolbox and take ten things out.
Name each and say what it does. Guessing is allowed.
Put them all back where they came from.

steps.test: Use a hammer, a saw and a screwdriver safely.
Use a drill safely and put it away properly.
Put every tool back clean and where it lives, all season.
steps.note: Where it lives means the same place every time, so the next person can find it.

steps.test: Choose the right tool for a job without asking anybody.
Teach tool safety to younger children.

tracks.name: Bike mechanics
tracks.line: Pumping a tyre to a full service.

steps.test: Pump a tyre to the right pressure.
Put a chain back on and clean your hands afterwards.
Mend a puncture so it holds.
Adjust brakes so they bite properly.
steps.note: The brakes should bite before the lever reaches the handlebar, and the wheel should still spin freely.

steps.test: Take a wheel off and put it back on true.
Service somebody else's bike so they can ride it safely.

tracks.name: First aid
tracks.line: Calling for help to being the one they turn to.

steps.test: Know how to call for help and exactly what to say.
how: 999 in the UK and Ireland, and ask for ambulance, fire or police.
Say where you are first — the address before anything else.
Then what happened, how many people, and stay on the line.

steps.test: Clean and cover a cut properly.
Treat a burn, a sting and a nosebleed correctly.
Put somebody in the recovery position.
steps.note: The recovery position keeps somebody breathing if they are unconscious. Learn it from a real course or a first aid site.

steps.test: Pass a real first aid course.
Be the person the group turns to when somebody is hurt.

tracks.name: How things work
tracks.line: Taking one apart to putting it back.

steps.test: Take something broken apart and name five parts inside.
Explain how one everyday machine works, correctly.
steps.note: A kettle, a bicycle gear, a toilet cistern or a door lock. Say it in order — what happens first, then what.

steps.test: Take something apart and put it back so it still works.
Find out why something stopped working and say why.
Repair a small motor or appliance.
Explain it to somebody else so they could do it.

tracks.name: Staying safe
tracks.line: Your address to looking after others.

steps.test: Say your own address and a phone number from memory.
Know what to do if you get separated in a busy place.
Cross a road safely on your own, every time.
Know what to do in a fire and where everybody meets.
Judge a risk out loud before doing something, and change the plan.
steps.note: Say it out loud before you do it: what could go wrong, how likely, and what you will change.

steps.test: Be responsible for a younger child's safety for a whole day.

categories.name: Care and kindness
categories.line: Animals, younger ones, older people, giving, the community.

tracks.name: Animals
tracks.line: Feeding to raising.

steps.test: Feed an animal the right amount, every day, for a week.
how: Find out how much this animal should get. Guessing is how animals get ill.
Feed it at about the same time each day.
Fresh water every time as well, not just food.

steps.test: Do the unpleasant half of caring for one, not just the nice half.
Look after an animal completely, on your own, for a week.
Notice an animal is unwell before anybody says, and tell somebody.
steps.note: Off its food, hiding, breathing oddly, or just not behaving like itself. Say so early rather than waiting.

steps.test: Raise something from young.
Teach another child to care for an animal properly.

tracks.name: Younger ones
tracks.line: Including them to looking after a family.

steps.test: Notice a younger child on their own and bring them into the game.
Teach one younger child one thing you can do.
Look after a younger child for an hour and everybody is happy at the end.
steps.note: Happy at the end is the test, for both of you. An hour is enough to count.

steps.test: Get a younger child through their first hard walk, to the end, happy.
Run an activity for a group of younger children.
Look after a family who are new, through their whole first season.

tracks.name: Older people
tracks.line: Hello, to keeping it up.

steps.test: Say hello to somebody much older and shake their hand properly.
Visit somebody older and listen to them for an hour.
Do a job for a neighbour and take nothing for it.
Write down somebody's story from their own telling.
steps.note: Write it down as they said it, not tidied up. Ask when, where and who, and let them talk.

steps.test: Organise something for people who are on their own.
Keep it up for a year.

tracks.name: Giving
tracks.line: Sharing to a habit other people copy.

steps.test: Share something you actually wanted, before being asked.
Give away something you liked.
Raise money for something that is not for you.
steps.note: Not for you means you get nothing out of it, including the credit.

steps.test: Give a share of what you earned away on purpose.
Do something kind that nobody asked you to do.
Make giving a habit that somebody else starts copying.

tracks.name: Your own patch
tracks.line: One bit of litter to a whole shore.

steps.test: Pick up litter you walk past, without being asked.
Fill a bag from one beach or one path.
Look after one small public place for a month.
steps.note: One small place means the same place, more than once — a lane, a corner of a beach, a bus shelter.

steps.test: Get three other people to help you.
Organise a clean-up for the group.
Make it happen every season for a year.

tracks.name: Welcoming
tracks.line: Saying hello to running the welcome.

steps.test: Say hello first to somebody new, before they say it to you.
Show a new person where everything is.
Learn and use the names of five people you have just met.
Sit with somebody who came on their own.
Introduce two people to each other and get them talking.
steps.note: Introducing people properly means giving each of them something to say next.

steps.test: Run the welcome for a new family on their first day.

categories.name: Focus and calm
categories.line: Stillness, attention, sleep, cold, gratitude, doing hard things.

tracks.name: Sitting still
tracks.line: One minute to twenty.

steps.test: Sit completely still and quiet for one minute.
how: Sit somewhere comfortable and set a timer for one minute.
Hands still, feet still, eyes open or shut, whichever.
Your mind will wander. That is fine and not a failure.
One minute is longer than you think, and that is the point.

steps.test: Sit still for five minutes without fidgeting.
steps.note: Fidgeting includes scratching and shifting about. Notice it, stop, carry on.

steps.test: Sit for ten minutes and notice your own breathing.
Sit for twenty minutes.
Do it every morning for thirty days.
Lead five minutes of stillness for the group.

tracks.name: Attention
tracks.line: One task to deep work.

steps.test: Do one thing for ten minutes with nothing else going on.
how: Pick one thing and put everything else out of reach.
Set a timer for ten minutes and start.
If you drift, come back. Drifting is not failing.

steps.test: Do one thing for twenty-five minutes without stopping.
steps.note: Twenty-five minutes is one pomodoro. Phone in another room, not face down beside you.

steps.test: Work for an hour with no screen near you.
Notice yourself drifting and come back, on purpose, five times.
Do a whole morning of one thing.
Explain to somebody else how you get yourself to concentrate.

tracks.name: Sleep
tracks.line: Going to bed to running your own rest.

steps.test: Go to bed without a fight, seven nights running.
Get up at the same time seven days running.
Notice how you feel after a bad night, and say so.
Keep screens out of the last hour before bed for two weeks.
steps.note: The last hour means no screens at all. Read, talk, or do something with your hands.

steps.test: Run your own bedtime with nobody reminding you, for a month.
Explain what sleep does, and help somebody else fix theirs.

tracks.name: Doing hard things
tracks.line: Not giving up to choosing the hard one.

steps.test: Finish something you wanted to give up on.
Keep going for ten minutes after it stopped being fun.
steps.note: Ten minutes past the point where you wanted to stop. Notice how it feels afterwards.

steps.test: Try something you are bad at, in front of other people.
Fail at something publicly and go back and do it again.
Choose the harder of two options on purpose, and say why.
Help somebody else through the moment they want to quit.

tracks.name: Noticing the good
tracks.line: One thing to a habit.

steps.test: Say one good thing about today, out loud, at tea.
Do it every day for a week.
Thank somebody properly, to their face, for something specific.
steps.note: Specific means what they actually did, not 'thanks for everything'.

steps.test: Write a thank-you letter that somebody keeps.
Do the daily one for thirty days.
Start it at a table where nobody was doing it.

journey.name: Easy wins
journey.line: Every one of these is a decision rather than a skill. Minutes each, nothing to buy, nothing to learn first. Most people are surprised they had never done them.

journey.name: Courage, worth and asking
journey.line: Deliberately early. Once you can ask for things, walk into anywhere and hear no without flinching, a great many things that looked like they cost money turn out not to. This stage quietly changes what everything after it is worth.
